newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX May COB electricity ends higher, May PV down.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX May COB electricity ends higher, May PV down.

text.p: NYMEX May electricity futures contracts finished in different direction Thursday ahead of their expiration tomorrow amid softer physical power prices and forecasts of cooler readings in the Southwest.

While cash prices at the California-Oregon Border (COB) and the Palo Verde (PV) switchyard in Arizona eased from Wednesday's level, spot COB values are still at considerable premium above May COB futures, brokers and traders said.
Firm, peak COB power for next-day delivery fell only 50 cents to $1 to $17.50-19.00 a megawatt hour (MWh). PV power with same delivery terms fell a whopping $4 to $18.00-19.00.
May COB futures settled up 35 cents at $13.90 a MWh, erasing a loss of 25 cent loss. June COB finished up 36 cents at $12.71. Deferred COB contracts ended 25 to 40 cents higher.
May PV settled down 25 cents at $17.98 after traded between $17.75 and $18.20. June PV finished down five cents at $18.30. Other PV months ended up five to down seven cents.
Cash prices at PV took a bigger hit today than those at COB because more generating capacity in the Southwest returned to service from recent repair and maintenance outages, market sources said.

In the Southwest, two 750 megawatt (MW) units at the Navajo coal-fired power plant near Page, Ariz., a 360 MW unit at the Springville, Ariz., coal-fired power plant and a 540 MW unit at the San Juan coal-fired station in New Mexico resumed full output by early Thursday.
In the Northwest, two 550 MW units at the Jim Bridger generating complex in Wyoming and a 408 MW unit at the Craig power plant in Colorado were restarted Wednesday.
Traders and brokers generally agreed that May PV futures would continue their weakness due to falling demand and rising supply, but they are less certain direction of May COB.
Some players expect May COB would ease as cash prices continue to fall, but other said the still sharp difference between COB cash and futures prices would push the May contract even higher.
"Some people has been anticipating the impact of hydro to come later. There are still some people who stayed short," said one Houston futures trader.
Citing another factor for a possible rise in May COB Friday, an Oregon-based trader said, "There's not anymore units in the Northwest coming back soon."
NYMEX estimated 766 COB and 463 PV contracts were sold, compared with 581 COB and 830 PV lots yesterday.
